Trying to expand everyone's musical palate. My library's also been getting a bit stale, so why not. To get the ball rolling: for me, it's "Amon Tobin". The first time I'd heard his music was while waking up, one morning, after an all-nighter Q3A session, at my buddy's place. As kids, that was basically our lives: Quake III Arena, Starcraft and Diablo III. Polish family, good people. Older brother was kind of a shady dude, but very smart; a "some men just want to watch the world burn" kind of guy. His hobbies included: trying to hack his dad's desktop, breaking security systems for jokes, and shutting down/reporting online pedophiles to authorities. Like I said, good people.

Either way, I'm just letting you know the context upon which this music came to my ears: waking up to a huge ruckus, after randomly staying over at a friend's house, because we forgot to keep track of the time. His dad was also a coder, of sorts; a professional web designer, since before PHP and Javascript were even a thing. His musical tastes were insane, by the standards of the day. He was also a smart dude, and I respected his opinion on things. His music had wafted the house, in times past: albeit muffled and restrained. But this time, it was blaring. The whole house shook with bass, and I witnessed "Four Ton Mantis", for the first time in my naive little life— the song has been scrubbed off the internet, for sample clearance reasons, but can still be found here: http://www.amontobin.com/discography-album&name=Supermodified+%28Album%29.

Something clicked in my brain, that hadn't done so, ever before. Chills ran over my whole body, and I teared up in awe (not even an exaggeration)— I'd never heard anything like it. Remember: I was a shitty little kid who'd only heard his parent's classics (standard radio stuff like "The Beatles" and "Frank Sinatra", etc. My parents were old, when they had me). I'd been banging to BS like Eminem and Korn; I thought I was edgy and cool for listening to Linkin Park— it was pretty bad.

Anyways, this song (and consequently, album) rattled my brain like nothing else ever did. It was completely electronic. A technological manipulation of analog sound, in such a way that it achieved something that could not possibly be reproduced with any non-digital instrument. It literally changed me, as a person, for the rest of my life. Ever since then, I burned the resolve in to my brain, that I would work on music for a living. The fact that something so visceral could come out of what I perceived to be a cookie-cutter profession just blew me away. I wanted to live in that world.

I've been "doing" music for over a decade, now, professionally. Gave up on the idea of "being famous", etc, a long time ago; but still work in the field, behind the scenes, because it will always be an important part of my life. Working on changing professions, for reasons. But music will always be there. Either way, I highly recommend you grab his discography. Most of it might sound dated, by now: but it is a technical marvel, for what else was available, at the time. He's a piece of musical history, as far as I'm concerned.
